This effect simulates the blurring of a random moving camera. Focusing Blur: blurs the corners of the image to reproduce the astigmatism distortion of the lens. Intelligent Blur: finds the edges of the colors in the image and blurs them without clouding the rest of the image. Frost Glass: blurs the image by randomly sprinkling the incoming light through the frosted glass. Mosaic: divides the photograph into rectangular squares and reconstructs it by filling the squares with the average pixel value.

Filter (if this box is checked, it will be run before the job is sent to the print system). This field shows which filters are currently selected to be "pre-filtered" for KDEPrint. Pre-films process print files before they are sent to the actual print subsystem. The list shown in this field may be empty (default ). Pre-films process the job in order of the list (the filter on the previous processor). This is the sort of filter that the output of this filter is the input of the next filter. For example, if your file is ASCII text, and you want the "Multipage per Sheet" filter to process its output, the first filter must be the ASCII to PostScript processor. KDEPrint can use any external filter program that you can use through this interface. KDEPrint has a way of supporting some of the common filters. However, these filters need to be installed separately, independent of KDEPrint. Pre-films work with all print subsystems supported by KDEPrint (such as CUPS, LPRng and LPD), since they do not depend on it.

Note that you can change only if you run this module with superuser privileges (usually the root ). If you did not start the KDE System Settings with superuser privileges (the correct method), click the Modify button to gain superuser privileges. You will be prompted to enter the superuser password. Appearance In this section you can configure the KDM Login Manager's appearance, the language it should use and the graphical user interface style it should use. This language setting does not affect the user's language settings. Fonts Here you can choose which fonts the KDM Login Manager should use to display messages such as greetings and names. Background If you want to set a specific background for the login screen, this is where you can do it. Shutdown Here you can specify who can shutdown or restart the computer, and if the boot manager should be used. Users In this section you can select the users that will be given you to select a login user. Convenience Here you can specify a user who will be logged in automatically, who does not need to enter a password when logging in, and other convenience features. Cookies Cookies contain information that Konqueror (or other KDE applications that use HTTP) stores on your computer, as directed by a remote computer. This means that a web server can store information about you and your browsing activity on this computer for later use. You may not like this, as it violates privacy. However, cookies are useful in certain circumstances. For example, cookies are often used by web browsers, allowing you to "put things in shopping baskets ". Some web sites require that you run a browser that supports cookie files. Since most people want to compromise between privacy and the benefits cookies provide, KDE allows you to customize how cookies are handled. You may want to set KDE's default policy to ask you whenever an external server wants to set up cookies, for you to decide; or you may want to simply accept or reject them all. For example, you may choose to accept all cookies made by your favorite shopping web site. To do so, simply browse to that web site, and when a cookie dialog box appears, click on this domain under the "Apply to" bar and select Accept, or simply identify the name of the web site in the domain-specific Policy bar and set it to Accept. This setting allows you to receive cookies from trusted web sites without being prompted each time KDE receives a cookie.

Cookies Cookies contain information that Konqueror (or other KDE applications that use HTTP) stores on your computer, as directed by a remote computer. This means that a web server can store information about you and your browsing activity on this computer for later use. You may not like this, as it violates privacy. However, cookies are useful in certain circumstances. For example, cookies are often used by web browsers, which allows you to "put things in a shopping basket ". Some web sites require you to run a browser that supports cookies. Since most people want to compromise between privacy and the benefits cookies provide, KDE allows you to customize how cookies are processed. You may want to set KDE's default policy to ask you whenever an external server wants to set cookies, for you to decide. For the favorite shopping web sites you trust, you may want to set the policy to accept, for you to visit those sites without being prompted whenever KDE receives cookies.

Focus Policy is used to determine the active window, i. e. the window where you can do something. Click to focus: A window becomes active when you click on it. You may be familiar with this application in another operating system. Focus by mouse: Moving the mouse pointer active on a standard window activates it. A new window gets a focus, and you do not need to point it explicitly. This is useful if you use the mouse often. Focus under mouse: The window below the mouse pointer is active. If the mouse pointer is pointing to nothing, the last window under the mouse will be focused. The window does not automatically get a focus. Focus under mouse accurately: Only the window below the mouse pointer is active. If the mouse pointer is pointing to nothing, nothing is focused. Note that " Focus under mouse " and " Focus under mouse accurately " prevent some features from functioning properly, for example the Alt+Tab window pass dialog in KDE mode.

The NFS and Samba Status Monitor are the frontiers of the smbstatus and showmount programs. Smbstatus announces Samba connections, and belongs to the Samba toolkit, which implements the SMB (session message block) protocol, also known as NetBIOS or LanManager. This protocol can be used to provide a printer or disk sharing service on a network containing MS Windows operating systems. Showmount belongs to the NFS software package. NFS is a network file system, the way files are shared over a traditional network in UNIX systems. In this case the output of the showmount command - a localhost - is decomposed. On some systems, showmount is in the / usr/ sbin directory: check if your PATH environment variable guides to showmount.

No hidden This option is based on the option of the same name provided in IRIX NFS. Normally, if a server exports two file systems, one of which is mounted to the other, the client must mount each file system separately to access it. If it mounts only the parent, it will encounter only an empty folder where the other file system is mounted, because it is "hidden". Setting the "no hidden" option to the file system causes it to be unhidden: properly recognized clients can switch between the parent and the sub-file systems, without any changes being detected. However, some NFS clients cannot handle this situation, for example, showing two files that appear to be on the same file system and have the same inode number. The "no hidden" option is currently only effective for single-host exports. It does not yet work for network group, subnet, or wildcards. This option may be very useful in some cases, but it is recommended to use it with care, only after confirming that the client system can manage the case correctly.

This determines how KWin will attempt to prevent focus from being eaten by unexpected new window activation. (Note: this feature does not work with either Focus Under Mouse or Focus Under Mouse Policy.) None: The stop is disabled, so the new window will always be active. Low: Stop is enabled: when a window does not have support for the underlying mechanism and KWin cannot decide whether to shut it down or not, it will be activated. This setting may result in both better and worse than the standard, depending on the window's application. Standard: Stop is enabled. High: The new window will be activated only if there is no currently active window, or if it belongs to an currently active application. This setting may not be very useful when you are not using the mouse focus policy. Very high: each window must be explicitly activated by the user. Windows prevented from eating focus will be marked as an active requirement, which by default means that their taskbar entry will be highlighted. This behavior can be changed in the Notifications control module.

KPhotoAlbum does not understand this concept, and of course, in order to make some plugins work KPhotoAlbum behaves with the plugin system as if they were. KPhotoAlbum does so by defining the current album as the current view & i. e. all images the browser will display. In addition to the current album, KPhotoAlbum must also be able to provide a list of all albums defined in this way: When KPhotoAlbum's browser displays the contents of a category, e. g. , People, each item in this category will appear as an album to the plugin. Otherwise KPhotoAlbum will use the category you defined with this option: e. g. , if you specify People with this option, KPhotoAlbum will behave as if you had just selected to show People, then call the plugin that needs to know about all albums. Perceptual intent causes the entire image to be compressed or expanded to take up the entire target device, so that gray balance may not be preserved, but colorimetric accuracy may not be preserved. That is to say, if certain colors in an image are outside the range of colors the output can draw, the image intent causes all colors in the image to be adjusted so that all colors in the image are within the range of colors that can be drawn, and the relationship between the different colors is preserved as much as possible. This intent is appropriate for displaying photographs and images, and is the default intent. Absolute colorimetric intent causes colors outside the range of colors the output can draw to be adjusted to the closest possible color to be drawn, and to remain unchanged. This intent preserves the white point and is very appropriate for spot colors (Pantone, TruMatch, icon colors, etc.). Relative colorimetric intent is defined so that colors outside the range of colors the output can draw to be adjusted to the closest possible color to be drawn, and to remain unchanged. Proof intent does not preserve the white point. Saturation intent preserves the saturation of the colors in the image at the expense of hue and lightness. This intent is not yet realized, and the ICC still develops the desired effect method. This intent is best suited for corporate graphics such as diagrams, which are more important to have vivid and contrasting colors than to have a high-quality individual color.

File Link This module allows users to select an application to open a certain type of file. The file type can also be a MIME (MIME stands for "Multipurpose Internet Mail Extensions".) A file link includes: Rules that allow you to determine the MIME of a file, for example the filename pattern *.kwd, meaning 'all files ending in.kwd', associated with the MIME type 'x-kword'. A short description of the MIME type, for example the description of the MIME type 'x-kword' is 'KWord Document'.) An icon that displays files with the MIME type, so that users can easily identify the file type, for example when viewing in Konqueror (at least for commonly used formats); A list of applications that can be used to open files with the MIME type. If there are several applications, a list is given in the priority range. You may be surprised to see that some MIME types do not have a filename pattern; in this case, Konqueror can still determine the MIME type by checking the file contents.

Job Priority Normally, CUPS prints the jobs in each queue according to the FIFO principle: First in, first out. The job priority feature allows you to reorder the queue, depending on the need. It works in both directions: you can increase and decrease the priority. (Oftentimes you can control only your jobs.) Since the default job priority is "50", any sent job with priority (e.g., "49") will be printed only after other jobs have been printed. Conversely, a job with a priority of "51" or more will be printed before jobs with a smaller priority. Perceptual intent causes the entire range of the image to be compressed or expanded to take up the entire range of the destination device, so that gray balance may not be preserved, but colorimetric accuracy may not be preserved. That is to say, if certain colors in an image are outside the range of colors the output device can draw, the image intent causes all colors in the image to be adjusted so that all colors in the image are within the range of colors that can be drawn, and the relationship between the different colors is preserved as much as possible. This intent is best suited for displaying photographs and images: it is the default intent. Absolute colorimetric intent causes colors outside the range of colors the output device can draw to be adjusted to the closest possible color to be drawn, and to remain unchanged. This intent preserves the white point and is best suited for spot colors (Pantone, TruMatch, icon colors, etc.). Relative colorimetric intent is defined so that colors outside the range of colors the output device can draw to be adjusted to the closest possible color to be drawn, and to remain unchanged. Proof intent does not preserve the white point. Saturation intent preserves the saturation of the colors in the image at the expense of hue and lightness. This intent is not yet realized, and the ICC still develops the desired effect method. This intent is best suited for corporate graphics such as diagrams, which are more important to have vivid and contrasting colors than to have a high-quality individual color.

When KDE starts, some checks are needed to check the system configuration (MIME type, installed applications, etc.), and if the configuration has changed since the last run, the system configuration cache (KSyCoCa) needs to be updated. This option prevents checks from being done, preventing scanning all directories containing system configuration files when KDE starts, thus making KDE start faster. However, in rare cases where the system configuration has changed since the last run, and changes are necessary before this delayed check, this option may cause some problems (lack of applications in the KMenu, notifications of applications about missing MIME types, etc.) Changes in system configuration are usually caused by installing or removing applications. This option should therefore be disabled temporarily when installing or removing applications.
